https://www.politico.eu/article/brussels.text: More drones in Europe’s skies might not sound like the obvious recipe for consensus among EU ministers. Yet, lifting a long-standing ban on spraying pesticides from uncrewed aerial vehicles is the least controversial part of the European Commission's overhaul of the bloc's pesticide rules — and one that the EU member countries have been seeking for years. While drones tend to carry negative connotations, given their deadly use in war or the ongoing airspace violations on the EU's eastern borders, their mission does not have to involve death and destruction. Advertisement Advertisement Since the 2010s, agricultural drones have taken off worldwide, going from novelty to standard farming tool in less than a decade. Visit any major agricultural fair and you’ll see high-tech drones stealing the spotlight once occupied by tractors and plows. The only catch? European farmers can admire them, but they can't actually use them — outside of very specific cases. Brussels is looking to change that. "Europe has the talent & technology to lead in digital agriculture. Now we need to make sure farmers benefit from it," Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen wrote on Bluesky Tuesday, mentioning drones specifically. The use of agricultural drones in the EU is governed not only by aviation law, like other drones, but also by a 2009 Directive on the Sustainable Use of Pesticides , which bans aerial spraying. But that framework is aimed at limiting spray drift, environmental contamination and exposure risks from crop-dusting planes and helicopters, written long before drones entered the farming mainstream. In practice, capitals can give farmers permission to spray pesticides only where it's hard or even dangerous to apply them directly. Think terraced vineyards in Portugal, apple orchards in South Tyrol, or flooded fields where tractors cannot operate and workers carrying backpack sprayers face a greater exposure risk. Supporters argue that this process is cumbersome — and that drones' benefits extend far beyond these niche cases and that the EU is lagging behind on farm tech. Drones can scan fields, spot pests and water stress earlier, and apply fertilizers and pesticides with far greater precision. By targeting only affected areas, they can reduce chemical use, lower costs, and limit environmental and health impacts, the argument goes. Pesticide lobby CropLife points out that drones are primarily battery-powered, making them a lower-emissions choice than tractors. Yet agricultural drones are caught in a loop of uncertainty, the Commission concedes in a document outlining the rationale for the omnibus proposal . "Important knowledge gaps remain" on how drones can be used safely — for example, it's not clear just how far pesticides will drift and which drones can most accurately deposit chemicals. Advertisement Advertisement At the same time, current restrictions on drone application make it difficult to learn more. The Commission acknowledges sector complaints that "drones are the technology most held back by the current framework, even though drones could contribute to more sustainable pesticide use." The regulatory framework might still be taking shape, but the Commission is already thinking big. Its Digital Strategy for Agriculture, expected by the end of the year, aims to put Europe at the forefront of the transition to so-called precision farming. Christophe Hansen speaks during an interview in Brussels on March 28, 2025. | John Thys/AFP via Getty Images "AI, satellites, drones & precision farming can boost productivity, use resources more efficiently & cut red tape," Hansen said in Tuesday's social media post. Give us drones EU member countries' first shot at reform of the outdated regulation became collateral damage in the political battle over the bloc's pesticide reduction law, which was eventually shelved in 2024 . In December 2024, 15 capitals, including Prague, asked the Commission to draw up a fresh drones proposal. The interest from the farmers' side has been growing steadily, particularly as they are being asked to reduce risks connected to the use of pesticides, according to the Czech Agriculture Ministry. Drones are "tools that can help reduce the amount of products applied, limit their impacts on non-target organisms, and at the same time maintain competitive agricultural production," said spokesperson Vojtěch Bílý. Advertisement Advertisement EU rules should enable drone spraying when the "risks are no greater than those associated with ground-based application," he added. The easy part In response to calls from member countries, the Commission has folded the proposal to relax rules on the use of drones into its wider food and feed safety omnibus — a politically contentious package that is otherwise triggering heavy resistance. Among the main points of contention in both Council and Parliament: unlimited approvals for all but the most hazardous active substances and a prohibition on agricultural imports with even a trace of some pesticides that can't be used in the U.S. Under the proposed overhaul for agricultural drones, member countries would be able to authorize their broader use, provided they are deemed no riskier than traditional ground-based spraying. While the Commission wants to give itself time to set out technical guidelines, the Council agreed in May to hand governments more immediate freedom to greenlight drones. Relative to the other parts of the omnibus, complaints from environmental groups have been relatively muted. Echoing the Commission’s concerns about unsettled science, environmental groups caution that regulators should move more slowly before authorizing drone spraying for broad categories of pesticides. Critics also raise concerns over data privacy and the potential for costly technology to widen the gap between large farms and smaller operators. These concerns didn't hold capitals back from backing broader drone use, and it doesn't seem to be sparking much debate in the Parliament ahead of a likely fall vote. Yet the full omnibus must be adopted as a package, and the Irish presidency still has no clear path to a compromise on the more contentious elements. If the whole measure founders, updates to drone rules will once again fall victim to a wider political fight. Advertisement Advertisement

Beállítom „4,3 milliárd forintot fizetett vissza az államnak a dr. Kőnig Róbert által alapított alapítvány” – jelentette be Hegedűs Zsolt egészségügyi miniszter egy Facebook-posztban . Hegedűs azt írta, hogy az Egészségtudatossági és Pácienstájékoztatási Alapítvány, amelyet Kőnig Róbert, Orbán Viktor betegtájékoztatásért és a betegelégedettség fejlesztéséért felelős miniszterelnöki biztosa alapított, 4,8 milliárd forintos támogatást kapott 2025 végén. Ebből az alapítvány már 4,3 milliárd forintot fizetett vissza, és a fennmaradó összeg felhasználásának tételes elszámolása folyamatban van. Hegedűs szerint az alapítvány célja, az egészségértés és a pácienstájékoztatás egyértelműen a betegek érdekeit szolgálják, de az állami támogatásból tervezett fejlesztéseket nem előzte meg szakmai egyeztetés az egészségügyi ágazat irányításával és a betegszervezetekkel. Kőnig 2026 májusában azt közölte, hogy a megítélt támogatásnak csak kisebb részét használták fel, és az alapítvány a teljes összeggel tételesen elszámol. Az eredetileg megítélt támogatás és a visszafizetett összeg közötti különbség hozzávetőleg 496,6 millió forint. „A közel 4,8 milliárd forintos támogatás nyilvánosságra kerülése után a Betegszervezetek Magyarországi Szövetsége is kritikát fogalmazott meg a támogatási rendszerrel kapcsolatban. A szervezet arra hívta fel a figyelmet, hogy miközben az újonnan létrehozott alapítvány jelentős állami forráshoz jutott, számos, régóta működő betegszervezet komoly forráshiánnyal küzd” – írta a miniszter. Az egészségügyi minisztérium korábban a Közép- és Kelet-európai Onkológiai Akadémia Alapítvány megszüntetéséről döntött . Az alapítványt 2019-ben hozta létre az akkori kormány, kuratóriumát éveken át Kásler Miklós vezette. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Judith Clark at Bedford Hills Correctional Facility for Women in New York State, 2017. Photograph: Damon Winter/New York Times/Redux/eyevine View image in fullscreen Judith Clark at Bedford Hills Correctional Facility for Women in New York State, 2017. Photograph: Damon Winter/New York Times/Redux/eyevine Home Office Shabana Mahmood urged to grant visa to former Weather Underground activist Home Office refused entry to Judith Clark, 77, invited by RSC to speak about restorative justice after her time in prison Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.34 EDT Last modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 12.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Human rights activists and celebrities including the lawyer Helena Kennedy, the actor Harriet Walter and the theatre director Phyllida Lloyd have urged the Home Office to overturn its decision to refuse a visa to a former member of the radical US group the Weather Underground, saying her decades of rehabilitation should count in her favour. Judith Clark, 77, was the inspiration for Walter’s portrayal of prisoners in the Donmar Warehouse all-female Shakespeare trilogy, including Brutus in Julius Caesar and Prospero in The Tempest. Clark had been invited to speak about rehabilitation and restorative justice at a Royal Shakespeare Company production of Julius Caesar in Stratford-upon-Avon next month, but her application to visit Britain was refused last week. She had also hoped to attend the UK launch of her daughter Harriet Clark’s first novel, The Hill , on 5 November. View image in fullscreen Judith Clark is escorted into Rockland county courthouse in New City, November 1981. Photograph: David Handschuh/AP Kennedy said that while the Home Office had rules governing visas for people with serious criminal convictions, there was also ministerial discretion, which should be exercised in Clark’s case. “This is a woman in her 70s who served a long sentence for political activism, which involved no violence on her part, and whose clear remorse and exceptional works within the prison system led to her early release,” she said. “She was deemed to pose no threat to US society and in my view she poses no threat whatsoever to the UK’s national security.” Living in a woman’s body: I left prison, but can’t forget how it feels when desire is criminalised Read more Walter said immigration rules designed to protect the public should allow flexibility in exceptional cases such as Clark’s. “There is no other purpose behind the short visit she wants to make other than to reward us with her presence as a speaker in our post-show conversation and to celebrate her daughter’s first book launch,” she said. Lloyd said Clark had become a touchstone for the creative team’s understanding of repentance, redemption and rehabilitation during the making of the Donmar trilogy. “To say she did her time and turned her life around is an understatement,” she said. “To have her speak in the UK would be an inspiration in the realm of restorative justice.” Clark joined the student movement against the Vietnam war in the late 1960s and became involved in the Weather Underground, a radical organisation that emerged from the American anti-war movement. She was later involved in the May 19th Communist Organization, which pursued armed revolutionary activity. View image in fullscreen Judith Clark escorted by officials in 1981. Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann Archive In 1983, she was convicted for her role as a getaway driver in an attempted robbery of a Brinks armoured truck in New York in 1981, during which a security guard and two police officers were killed. She was sentenced to three consecutive terms of 25 years to life. In 2017, the then-New York governor Andrew Cuomo commuted her sentence, allowing her to seek parole. She was released in 2019, after serving 37 years. During her incarceration at Bedford Hills correctional facility in New York, Clark helped establish an Aids education and support group, developed programmes to help mothers maintain relationships with their children, raised service dogs for veterans and first responders and helped build a college education programme. She has since worked in criminal justice reform and support for formerly incarcerated women. In 2025, she became director of the Survivors Justice Project, which works to secure legal relief for survivors of domestic violence facing prison sentences. Walter and Lloyd met Clark while researching their Shakespeare trilogy, which reimagined the plays as productions staged by women in prison. Walter said Clark had helped her understand Brutus, the politically conflicted character in Julius Caesar, who struggles with the moral consequences of his actions. Her story also informed Walter’s portrayal of Prospero in The Tempest. “By the time I met Judy she had developed into one of the most exemplary and evolved human beings I have ever met or am likely to meet,” Walter said. The RSC has invited Clark to take part in a post-show discussion entitled Can Art Save Lives? Harriet Clark spent a lifetime visiting her mother, an ex-Weather Underground member, in prison: ‘The US has always used family separation to destabilize’ Read more It would also include a company member introduced to theatre after prison through the charity Clean Break. Kennedy first met Clark more than 30 years ago at Bedford Hills while making a television documentary about women in prison. “Her remorse for her participation in criminal conduct was very evident to all who were involved with her,” she said. In her own letter supporting her visa application, Clark said she had publicly disavowed her actions and apologised for the harm she had contributed to a decade into her sentence. She spent the remainder of her imprisonment trying to turn her remorse into work benefiting the prison community, families and those harmed by crime. Clark hoped to visit Britain from 4 to 15 November with her wife, Cheryl Moch. Her daughter has said that The Hill draws on her own experience of visiting her mother throughout her imprisonment. Despite their separation, she wrote, Clark had found ways to mother her. A Home Office spokesperson said: “It’s our longstanding policy not to comment on individual cases. “All applications for entry clearance in the UK are carefully considered on their individual merits, in line with the Immigration Rules and based on the information and evidence provided by the applicant.” Explore more on these topics Home Office Theatre Human rights Harriet Walter Prisons and probation UK criminal justice Royal Shakespeare Company news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries
